articles.title: Celia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing show
articles.summary: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection. Burberry and Celia Birtwell are both national treasures of sorts.
body: Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closed London fashion week was born.

Burberry’s calling card is a graphic check; Birtwell is all blowsy doodled florals and psychedelic snaking vines. “The check is so dominant and so brilliant that at first I thought: what can I do here?” Birtwell said before the show. She hand-painted a less regimented version, which Lee loved. “She made the check more human. If you are buying a luxury product it’s not a necessity, it’s an emotional purchase, so it needs to feel human.” A doodle of round, Smartie-bright faces from her archive, drawn 20 years ago but never produced, became another print of the season.

The mood of the show, held around the corner from Burberry HQ at Chelsea School of Art, was buoyant: charming prints, soft silhouettes, and the eclectic guest list that is as much a Burberry signature as the check itself: actor Fiona Shaw and footballer Djed Spence on the front row, with rapper Central Cee making a cameo on the catwalk.
points: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection.

articles.title: The best plastic-free cutting boards: I spent six weeks testing 10 boards, and these won
articles.summary: A good, sturdy chopping board will last you many years. I tested the best non-plastic, non-toxic ones, including some made out of wood and synthetic rubber. A cutting board is literally the foundation of most things you cook.
body: Plastic cutting boards are affordable and convenient, but research shows they shed significant amounts of microplastics into food. And though the health damage caused by microplastics is still being studied, we don’t need microplastics in our minestrone.

Many people believe that plastic cutting boards are more hygienic, but a study from the Journal of Consumer Protection and Food Safety found only minor differences “in microbiological counts” on wooden and plastic chopping boards “after proper cleaning” ( how to clean a cutting board ). Plastic boards also tend to get scratched up more than their natural alternatives.

To help you avoid plastics, I tested a bunch of non-toxic, plastic-free cutting boards in my home. Good chopping boards should be sturdy, gentle on kitchen knives, easy to clean and versatile. My picks are below.

articles.title: Is it true that … cycling affects fertility?
articles.summary: Saddling up is only likely to be an issue for elite athletes – and those with low sperm counts. “Cycling isn’t big on the radar of fertility doctors,” says Prof Colin Duncan, a fertility expert at the University of Edinburgh.
body: For women, he says, the only time cycling is likely to affect fertility is when it’s done at extreme levels, such as the kind of training undertaken by elite athletes.
“Doing huge amounts of physical activity can lower body fat, and that can switch off the ovaries,” he says. “Elite athletes may stop having their periods and reduce their fertility.”

For men, things are a little different. Sitting on a bicycle saddle for prolonged periods can increase the temperature around the testicles, “almost incubating them”. This can affect sperm production, because sperm develop best at a cooler temperature – one reason the testicles are located outside the body.
But for most men, Duncan says, this isn’t something to worry about. “The testicles produce way more sperm than is actually required for fertility.

articles.title: Get tested and talk to your partner: how to have safer sex after age 50
articles.summary: At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide. When I got divorced after 28 years of monogamy, I was excited to be having sex again, but had concerns.
body: Now, at 51, I’ve been wondering how important barrier protection is for me. Though I haven’t hit menopause, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says that “by 45 getting pregnant naturally is unlikely”, and HIV/Aids prevention and treatment have improved significantly in the last three decades.
When I consulted with my physician, she said I should still “be careful” but didn’t provide specific guidelines.

Frustrated, I started researching. I found books on safer sex for older adults, such as Never Too Late: Your Guide to Safer Sex after 60 by Dr Shannon Dowler. But I wanted something more concise, like the pamphlets we saw as teens. I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide, with expert advice about how to have safer sex as an older adult.
No sex is totally risk-free – at any age. This reality is reflected in the American Medical Association (AMA) using the term “safer sex” since the mid-90s, rather than “safe sex”.

articles.title: Here's What It's Like Shadowing a Blacksmith at Ashford Castle in Ireland—and How to Book the Experience Yourself
articles.summary: Writer Sarah Wood González visited the Guinness family’s former Irish estate—now one of Ireland's most iconic castle hotels—to try her hand at blacksmithing.
body: I can’t stop talking about blacksmithing. Any time I’ve run into someone in the last year, I’ve found some way to bring it up. Perhaps it’s a symptom of my obsession with the Middle Ages, or an effect of my brother being a welder, or maybe a function of my interest in age-old crafts as a way to counterbalance my anxiety about the unknown future.

That’s all to say, when I learned that Ashford Castle —the historic Guinness family estate turned iconic luxury hotel in County Mayo, Ireland —offers an experience where you can shadow a blacksmith for a day, I leapt at the opportunity. I booked the “Fire & Wood” itinerary within the hotel's Meet the Makers program, designed to help guests connect with authentic local crafts and culture, as part of an August stay with my mom. Next thing I knew, I was flying out to the Irish countryside.

articles.title: How to Live the Real La Dolce Vita, According to Italy’s “Pasta Grannies”
articles.summary: Vicky Bennison, the author and creator of “Pasta Grannies,” shares the wisdom—and a favorite recipe—of the older women keeping Italian culinary traditions alive.
body: What would it be like to learn the recipes—and life wisdom—of hundreds of Italian grandmothers?

Vicky Bennison can tell you. As the creator of the Pasta Grannies online community and documentary series, Bennison has interviewed more than 500 senior women throughout Italy, bringing millions of people into the kitchens of beloved nonne. The London-based Bennison first started the Pasta Grannies YouTube channel in 2014, after years of living part-time in the Marche region of Italy, where she noticed that the older generation seemed to be the only ones still making pasta by hand.
“I thought: Who’s making a record of all this?” she tells Vogue.

Though Italian chefs often credit their grandmothers, mothers, or aunts as teachers, Bennison realized that these vital culinary figures were “never seen,” she says. “These women are the cornerstone of Italian cuisine, and they’re just invisible.”

articles.title: Savory Dutch Baby
articles.summary: Is there any time of day when a pancake isn’t welcome at the table? What about a Savory Dutch Baby that mixes up in seconds? Didn’t think so.
body: Essentially a giant popover, this savory Dutch baby emerges from the oven dramatically puffed, with crisp edges and a tender, eggy center. A blender makes quick work of the batter, while a little cornstarch helps create that contrast in textures. Don’t be alarmed when it begins to deflate after leaving the oven—that’s exactly what it’s supposed to do.
Top your Dutch baby with fried eggs, avocado, and shaved ham; smoked salmon, crème fraîche, and sliced scallions; or sautéed kale, crispy bacon, and aged cheddar.

A properly preheated skillet is key: This recipe heats the pan in a 450° oven for at least 25 minutes so the batter starts cooking as soon as it hits the surface. Room-temperature ingredients and whipping plenty of air into the eggs also encourage a good rise. And remember, your Dutch baby will naturally deflate after it comes out of the oven.

A blender quickly incorporates air into the eggs, helping the Dutch baby puff. No blender? Several Bon Appétit readers have successfully made this recipe using a whisk; beat the eggs vigorously until very frothy before adding the remaining ingredients.

articles.title: This Cult London Jewelry Brand Wants to Turn Your Home Into an Heirloom
articles.summary: Presenting at London Fashion Week, jewelry studio founder and NewGen recipient Toby Vernon is expanding The Ouze’s raw, modern sensibilities into homeware.
body: On the third day of London Fashion Week, The Ouze staged its third Newgen presentation at 180 Studios. Previous seasons saw Vernon curate the subterranean room into messy domestic tableaux, with pieces nestled among scenes of dinner parties and unfinished musical manuscripts—the detritus of a chaotic creative process. For spring 2027, he brought visitors into another part of jewelry making that is rarely seen.

The dominant color of the room was not sterling silver, ruby, or emerald, but Yves Klein blue. Jewelry sat on and among a sink, chair, cabinet, artist easel, and smaller domestic objects coated in the blue carving wax Vernon uses in the workshop. Every piece from The Ouze begins this way, hand-carved in wax before being translated into precious metal. There are many grades and colors used in jewelry making, but this particular striking blue was the first Vernon worked with. “It’s not too brittle, it’s not too weak, and it’s an amazing color,” he says. “It’s just very important to the brand and the way the jewelry’s made.”

articles.title: ‘There a Bit of Eliza Doolittle in Me’: Twiggy on Her Unlikely Story—and New Documentary
articles.summary: The model and actor is the focus of a new documentary by Sadie Frost. Here, subject and director discuss how “Twiggy” came to be.
body: When I speak to Twiggy, we’re sitting near the back of a quiet Italian restaurant in Chelsea. It’s a beautiful late-summer day, and people are enjoying lunch on the sunlit terrace.

Twiggy—who achieved global fame at just 16 years old, becoming arguably the world’s first true supermodel—is in the midst of a busy week: last night, she hosted a screening party at Sloane’s in SoHo for a new documentary about her life, where guests like Fran Drescher, Ellen von Unwerth, Iris Law, and Donna Karan paid her tribute. In a few days, she’ll be in Los Angeles, hosting another screening.
Before this trip, Twiggy, now 77, hadn’t visited New York since before the pandemic. The very first time she touched down here, however, she was 17 and immediately mobbed by fans.
“I landed and they were teenage girls with banners up with my name,” she remembers. “I came in after the Beatles, so I became part of the British Invasion... I was one of the invaders.”

articles.title: The Bride Wore a Pearlescent, Ocean-Inspired Wardrobe for Her Harbour Island Wedding
articles.summary: Interior designer Bella Pepin took inspiration from pearls, shells, raffia, and fish motifs for her unique wedding weekend wardrobe, marrying Cameron Kenny in the Bahamas.
body: The vision for the weekend was to have a unique, elevated design perspective, without it feeling too serious. “Island-y, but not beach-y,” explains Bella. “All of our events were outdoors—with the exception of a rehearsal dinner pivot due to rain—so we wanted the designs to mimic natural Caribbean elements, sticking to a color and material palette seen in the surrounding tropical landscape.” The bride also put particular care into the invitations and paper goods throughout the weekend, hiring calligrapher Emily Snyder to create playful illustrations for the designs. The bride adds, “The kissing fish she doodled are everything to me!”

articles.title: An Expert Guide To Planning a K-Beauty Trip To South Korea
articles.summary: Korea’s beauty tourism is booming—here's how to get the most out of your K-beauty treatment trip, according to skincare specialists.
body: If you'd told me when I was 13 years old, a half-Korean girl growing up in Canada, that Korean beauty products would one day line the shelves of every Sephora around the world, I wouldn’t have believed you. The Korean Wave–K-pop, K-beauty, K-entertainment, and K-food–has spread globally over the past two decades but, recently, it seems to have reached a crescendo. From Olive Young opening its first North American location in Pasadena, California, this summer to the frequently sold-out kimbap at my local Trader Joe’s, Korean culture is everywhere.

This year, I was one of them. Well, sort of. I went to Korea to explore my father’s native country. But after six weeks of witnessing age-defying complexions, I figured when in Rome. I had scouted Seoul’s K-beauty scene back in 2024, but with the industry’s rapid development, I was due for a follow-up. After several clinic visits, treatments, and interviews with Seoul- and New York-based Korean experts—here’s what I wish I’d known earlier.
